purpose: Owner answers 249a, 250a and 251a of 5 November 2026: StudyMapForCombinedEvidence keeps the studies behind a conclusion that combines them as a small study map, CommunityToFormalHypothesisTransfer counts one report of a cheap, low-risk option the answer doesn't yet cover as high-value, and ReportQualityBesideCounts and SharedMechanismSearch say how good people's reports are and search each way an option could work.

<Rule name="CommunityToFormalHypothesisTransfer">
   Turn repeated or high-value community observations into explicit formal-search hypotheses, transferring, as
   applicable: vernacular and historical terminology; intervention and ingredient identity; diet or exercise pattern;
   dose, route, formulation, timing, duration, and co-interventions; responder phenotype; baseline severity; rapid
   versus delayed time course; dechallenge and rechallenge; objective or functional outcomes; recurrence patterns;
   adverse effects; failure and discontinuation; and claimed mechanisms. Search indexed studies, trial registries,
   cohorts, case series, conference materials, theses, practitioner datasets, books, regulatory records, and citation
   chains with those leads. A new decision-relevant hypothesis reopens the relevant extended human-evidence source
   classes; the earlier sweep is not final. Say in the answer which community leads changed the study search, and what
   the studies then showed about them.
  </Rule>

<Rule name="DuplicateAndDataLineageAudit">
   Identify duplicate publications, overlapping cohorts, abstracts later published in full, repeated registry analyses,
   recycled case narratives, and practitioner datasets drawn from the same patients. Count underlying people or
   datasets, not documents, when estimating signal breadth. Marketing copy, retailer listings, articles, and press
   releases that repeat one trial are one lineage, not independent confirmation.
  </Rule>

  <Rule name="StudyMapForCombinedEvidence" priority="High">
   When a conclusion combines studies, or rests on something not found or not shown, keep the
   DuplicateAndDataLineageAudit as a small study map in finalize_research's later_inputs.study_map, from what the
   research read. Give each study its identifier, its trial registry number if any, and the group of people behind it:
   where and when they were recruited, how many, and who ran or paid for it. Link a study that shares people with,
   reanalyses, extends or is an abstract of another, and a review to the study it cites as evidence, each with the
   sentence that shows the link. Count groups of people, not papers. Compare a registered trial's paper with its
   registration from before the trial started: outcomes left out, added, or moved between primary and secondary without
   a reason the paper gives. Say in the answer what the map finds. Whether two groups overlap stays your judgment.
  </Rule>

<Rule name="ContextExtraction" priority="High">
   Extract diagnosis or symptom target, baseline trajectory, formulation, route, concentration or dose when available,
   duration, frequency, co-interventions, prior treatments, time to effect, persistence, stable disease, progression,
   adverse effects, discontinuation, withdrawal, rechallenge, and outcome measurement. Distinguish expected outcomes
   after concurrent standard care from changes temporally attributable to the intervention under review. For a brief
   symptom, record when it began and whether it ended without treatment, and keep a change in the target symptom apart
   from a change in a symptom that comes with it.
  </Rule>

  <Rule name="ReportQualityBesideCounts" priority="High">
   Beside how many people said an option worked, say how good their reports are: how many gave the details
   ContextExtraction lists, how many measured the change, and how many are bare one-liners. When the only plausible way
   an option works is expectation, such as soap under the pillow, say so, after naming any other way it could work, such
   as its scent.
  </Rule>

  <Rule name="SharedMechanismSearch" priority="High">
   For an option the research finds, name the ways it could work, and search each in studies and in people's reports,
   with the other options that work the same way: for the didgeridoo, the muscle tone of the upper airway, which mouth
   and throat exercises and singing also train, and humming, which raises the nitric oxide in the nose. A shared
   mechanism says what to search next; it never stands in for the option's own results (MechanismIsNotOutcome).
  </Rule>
